title: Rethinking Projector Training in Multimodal LLMs
claim: Standard training fits a projector on paired data, but many projectors work equally well, so a closed-form construction can replace training.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, colored headers, interpolation line in middle, distribution transport at right
description: Three rounded panels with colored title banners, read left to right as an argument. The left panel (blue) shows the standard pipeline as a vertical stack: Vision Encoder (frozen, snowflake icon) feeds a Projector (trainable, flame icon), then Vision Tokens, a Language Model (frozen) and Answer Tokens, with Question Tokens joining. A dashed legend explains the icons. A green arrow leads to the middle panel (green). There, Dataset A and Dataset B give trained projectors W_A and W_B. A parameter-space line interpolates between them with alpha values from 1 to 0, with the formula W(α)=αW_A+(1−α)W_B. A caption says all interpolated projectors perform well. The right panel (purple) shows Vision Encoder Space to Projector W (PORTAL) to Language Model Space. Below it, a blue distribution is mapped to a yellow one by an optimal-transport ellipse and green arrows.
caption: Projector alignment as a coarse alignment with a broad solution space. (Left) Standard pipeline: during projector alignment, the vision encoder and language model are frozen, and only the projector is trained to map visual tokens into a representation space compatible with the LLM using image-caption pairs. (Middle) We show that projectors trained on different image-caption datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving downstream performance, indicating that there is a large solution space for the weights of the projector. (Right) This observation motivates a closed-form solution of projector alignment. We propose a training-free projector \name constructed by optimal transport between the two modalities' marginal statistics.
abstract: Multimodal LLMs are typically trained by first aligning a vision encoder with a language model via projector training on large image-caption datasets, followed by joint training of the full multimodal model. Despite its widespread use, the role of the projector training stage remains poorly understood. We find that (i) using only $10$ to $20\%$ of the data for training the projector already recovers most downstream performance gains, and (ii) projectors trained on different datasets can be linearly interpolated while largely preserving performance. These results suggest that projector training mainly performs a coarse alignment, which many different projectors achieve equally well. Motivated by these findings, we propose PORTAL, a training-free projector initialization that requires neither paired image-caption data nor gradient-based optimization, but only per-modality summary statistics. PORTAL computes an optimal-transport-based map between Gaussian approximations of the vision and language feature distributions on a shared principal subspace, so that the projector training stage can be skipped entirely. Without any paired data, PORTAL matches the standard pipeline trained on 558k image-caption pairs across six LLM backbones, two vision encoders, and 16 benchmarks. It outperforms that pipeline in $3$ of $7$ (vision encoder, LLM) settings and reaches an average $98\%$ of its score across the other four.
